description: Team Obsidian Prime is a STEM initiative by Dreams of Bangladesh (DOB). We are passionate young innovators with a proven track record in autonomous robotics, embedded systems, and tech research (Gold Medalists at WICE 2026).
summary:
Baseline tells an astronaut whether today is normal for them. At Mars, a reply from Earth can take up to 40 minutes, so the crew must catch health changes themselves.

Baseline is a working offline web app for phone, tablet and laptop. Each day the astronaut does a 2-minute self-check: a reaction test, sleep hours, sleep quality, mood and a near-vision line. The app compares these answers and a wearable record (simulated here) with that person's own earlier days, up to 30.

When a reading leaves their usual range, the app shows what changed, the NASA study behind the flag and one step from a NASA source. The next day shows whether the reading came back. A flight surgeon view shows three crew members.

Fixed rules with tests raise the flags, not an AI model. Part of the app runs on real NASA and NOAA data. On Curiosity rover radiation data (MSL RAD), the rule fired on 20 May 2024: 1,881.0 µGy per day against a usual 161.0. The app replays a NOAA GOES solar storm and a Skylab 4 crew sleep record. It never names what is wrong, and all data stays on the device.
details:
The Why, the What, and the How

Why it is important

On a long mission, the crew must notice changes in their own body and mind. Help is far away. At Mars, a reply from Earth can come up to 40 minutes later. That is up to 20 minutes each way (NASA Human Research Program, Distance From Earth). A group average cannot say what is normal for one person. Baseline compares each crew member with their own normal.

What it does

  • Gather: The app collects a daily 2-minute self-check: reaction time, sleep, sleep quality, mood and a near-vision line. It adds a wearable record, which is simulated and labelled so on every screen. It also reads the radiation environment from NASA MSL RAD and NOAA GOES.
  • Evaluate: The app charts seven signals against the person's own usual range. They are heart rate, heart rate variability, blood oxygen, core temperature, sleep, mood and reaction time. A flag opens an evidence card. The card shows the numbers, the NASA study, how strong that study is, and "Show the maths".
  • Act: Each flag comes with one step from a NASA source and a "Mark step done" button. The app queues a summary for the flight surgeon and checks the reading again the next day.

How it works and how we tested it

  • The rule: A reading 2 to 3 spreads (standard deviations) from the person's usual is a watch item. At 3 or more spreads, or 2 or more on two days running, it is flagged. Two flagged signals within 48 hours raise one more flag. The usual range uses only earlier days, and no flag fires before day 15.
  • On simulated data: On 200 simulated records, the rules catch a 4-SD shift in at least 97% of records. A clean 30-day record raises 0.62 false flags on average.
  • On real data: We ran the sleep rule on the Skylab 4 crew's own sleep estimates, 84 nights each. It flags 2 nights for the commander, 2 for the pilot and 1 for the science pilot. We ran the radiation rule on the real Mars record of 20 April to 25 May 2024. It fires on 20 May 2024 only: 1,881.0 µGy per day against a usual 161.0.

Creativity and Factors Considered

How our project is creative

  • Own normal: We track each person against their own normal, not a group average.
  • "Show the maths": Each single-signal flag shows its own sum, so the user can check the maths by hand. No black-box model decides a flag.
  • Real data replays: Users can replay three real records through our rules. They are the Mars radiation surge of 20 May 2024, the solar storm of 9 September 2024 and the Skylab 4 crew sleep record.
  • A NASA source on every flag: Each of the 8 rules cites a NASA source. Two of them cite the Mars-500 ground isolation study in NASA OSDR. Each step also comes from a NASA source.

Factors and limits we considered

  • Offline: Baseline is a working offline web app on the phone, the tablet and the laptop. All data stays on the device. It is designed for a vehicle's own network, with no internet.
  • No medical advice: The app gives only routine NASA steps, such as exercise, a light schedule, or a report to the flight surgeon. Every line on screen passes a wording check with 76 blocked terms, so the app never names what is wrong.
  • Limits: The vital signs are simulated, and every screen says so. The radiation, the solar events and the Skylab 4 record are real. Blood pressure and blood sugar are not covered, because only simulated values would be possible.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Who benefits and the intended impact

  • Deep-space crews: Crew members far from Earth can act before help can reply. They see when a reading leaves their own usual range.
  • Flight surgeons: They see three crew members on one screen, each against their own normal, with the study and the step attached.
  • Earth analog missions: Crews could run the same daily check.
  • Open-source readers: Anyone who reads the code benefits, since the rules, tests and validation are open.

Tools and Technologies

Baseline is built in Python (rules, tests and scripts) and plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (the page, with no build step).

  • Libraries: numpy, requests, pytest and Chart.js 4.5.1 (MIT).
  • Testing: pytest runs 207 automated tests. Playwright drives a test browser for layout checks and screenshots.
  • Fonts: Source Sans 3 and JetBrains Mono (SIL Open Font License 1.1).
  • Hosting: Python's own web server, on the laptop or the local Wi-Fi, with no cloud. The public demo runs on GitHub Pages.
